keepalive.start: JSON-RPC camera.start_monitor over ws://{address}/websocket, params {req_id:<n>, domain:"lan", interval:0, expect_pw:false}. (HTTP transport is disabled for this method in the Snapmaker fork — WebSocket only.)

streams.name: built-in
streams.notes: A single JPEG the daemon overwrites. Poll with a cache-buster query (?ts=...) at ~1 fps. Frames only refresh while a monitor session is held (see keepalive). Verified live: image/jpeg, ~93 KB, frame-to-frame changes.

device.name: Snapmaker U1 Multi-Color 3D Printer
device.notes:
The Snapmaker U1 is a 2025/2026 CoreXY FDM printer with four independent toolheads for up to 4-color printing. Unlike Snapmaker's earlier machines (which used the SACP binary protocol or the Snapmaker 2.0 HTTP-token API), the U1 runs a stock-shaped Klipper + Moonraker + Fluidd stack (Snapmaker's own GPL forks, open-sourced 2026-03-30) on embedded Linux (Buildroot; internal user "lava"). Local control is therefore ordinary Moonraker: an HTTP REST API and a JSON-RPC-2.0-over-WebSocket API on port 80 (nginx fronts Moonraker's internal 7125; Orca falls back to 8080 for uploads).
NO CLOUD REQUIRED for local printing or monitoring. The device has an explicit LAN mode (mDNS TXT link_mode=lan) and, on stock firmware, moonraker.conf lists all RFC-1918 ranges in [authorization] trusted_clients — so any LAN client reaches the full REST/WebSocket API with no API key and no pairing. (An X-Api-Key header is accepted but not required.) The cert-pairing / secure-MQTT channel below only gates the unified transport that Snapmaker Orca and the mobile app prefer; it is not needed to drive the printer locally.
SECURE-MQTT SIDE CHANNEL (documented, not driven here): the U1 also runs an on-device Mosquitto broker — plain MQTT on 1884 (the port ADVERTISED over mDNS), mTLS on 8883 — mirroring the Moonraker JSON-RPC API over topics {SN}/request | {SN}/response | {SN}/notification | {SN}/status (SN = serial, uppercase). LAN pairing: connect to 1884, publish a JSON-RPC auth request to {access_code}/config/request (default access code 12345678), the user taps Approve on the touchscreen, and the device returns {ca, cert, key, port:8883} on {access_code}/config/response; the client then reconnects over mqtts://<ip>:8883 with the issued client certificate. This exists for parity with Orca and to survive a future firmware that might lock the HTTP API — the plain HTTP/WS path is the simpler local target today.
SAFETY: this is a heated FDM printer with motion. gcode/script and print control move real hardware and drive 200 C+ hotends; treat all writes as advanced and never issue them to a printer you are only monitoring.

issued_to_client: On the secure-MQTT path only: a CA + client cert/key, issued after touchscreen approval of access code 12345678
credentials.notes: The plain HTTP/WebSocket API needs no credential on the LAN (trusted_clients covers RFC-1918). The certificate scheme applies only to the secure-MQTT channel; the on-device CA (15-year validity) signs one client cert per approved client.
stored_on_device: Home Wi-Fi credentials (entered at the touchscreen)
Per-approved-client X.509 certificates for the secure-MQTT channel (mapping in printer_data/mqtt/client.json)

factory_reset.effect: Not documented here. A network/cloud unbind is available from the touchscreen; the machine stores no third-party credentials for the plain HTTP path.

methods.description: Join the U1 to Wi-Fi (or Ethernet) from its touchscreen; it then advertises _snapmaker._tcp and serves Moonraker on port 80.

steps.action: Connect the printer to the network from its touchscreen (LAN mode keeps it cloud-free).
Browse mDNS _snapmaker._tcp.local.; read TXT ip and sn (ignore the advertised port 1884 for HTTP).
GET http://<ip>/printer/info and /server/info to confirm Moonraker is up and Klipper is ready.

setup.notes: No provisioning is needed to control an already-networked U1: browse _snapmaker._tcp, read the TXT ip/sn (or resolve the U1-<SN>.local hostname), and hit Moonraker on http://<ip>/ — no auth on the LAN. Confidence high: verified live here, and matched by the ha-snapmaker-u1 integration which connects to port 80 with no key. IMPORTANT: the mDNS answer advertises port 1884 (the plain-MQTT LAN broker), NOT the HTTP port — a consumer must ignore the advertised port for REST/WebSocket and use 80 (fallback 8080 for uploads). Initial Wi-Fi onboarding is done at the printer's own touchscreen; there is no app-only step for local control.

rejoin.notes: Rejoin from the touchscreen. Clients should rediscover by mDNS TXT sn, not by cached IP, since DHCP may move the printer.

testing.notes: Read/monitor path verified live 2026-08-14 against a real U1 (Moonraker hostname "lava", software_version 1.5.1.2_20260703125508, Buildroot 2024.02, Klipper state ready) discovered by its _snapmaker._tcp mDNS advertisement and reached on plain HTTP port 80 with NO authentication (GET /server/files/list returned 200 without any API key, confirming the LAN-trusted-clients posture). Exercised as documented: GET /printer/info (state ready), GET /server/info (klippy_connected true), GET /printer/objects/list — which showed the four independent toolheads extruder/extruder1/extruder2/extruder3 plus per-nozzle heater fans, confirming the quad-hotend architecture — and GET /printer/objects/query returned live telemetry (heater_bed 27.0 C, extruder 29.0 C, print_stats.state "complete", display_status.progress 1.0: a finished print resting on the bed). The CAMERA was verified live: GET /server/webcams/list is empty (the stock camera is not a registered Moonraker webcam), but the daemon path works — camera.start_monitor over ws://<ip>/websocket returned notify_camera_status_change {monitoring:true}, after which GET /server/files/camera/monitor.jpg returned changing ~93 KB image/jpeg frames (a real interior view of the four toolheads). The REPRINT read path was verified too: /server/history/list returned 3 completed jobs (each with 3 thumbnails) and /server/files/list returned 7 gcode files whose paths feed /printer/print/start?filename=. NOT exercised (someone else's printer, left untouched): the print-control WRITES themselves — print/cancel, print/start, pause/resume, gcode/script, upload — and the secure-MQTT / cert-pairing channel (documented from the vendor forks only).

entities.name: Print State
entities.notes: standby / printing / paused / complete / error / cancelled.

http_endpoints.description: Klipper/host identity and readiness (state, hostname, software_version, cpu_info). Live-verified. JSON-RPC equivalent: printer.info.
http_endpoints.name: Printer Info

http_endpoints.description: Moonraker server state incl. klippy_connected and klippy_state and the loaded component list. Live-verified.
http_endpoints.name: Server Info

http_endpoints.description: Available Klipper objects. On the U1 this includes extruder, extruder1, extruder2, extruder3 (four toolheads), heater_bed, per-nozzle heater_fan e{0..3}_nozzle_fan, print_stats, virtual_sdcard, toolhead, display_status. Live-verified.
http_endpoints.name: List Printer Objects

http_endpoints.description: One-shot telemetry read, e.g. ?heater_bed&extruder&print_stats&display_status returns temperatures, print_stats.state and display_status.progress. Live-verified. For a live stream, use printer.objects.subscribe over the WebSocket.
http_endpoints.name: Query Objects

http_endpoints.description: G-code file listing. Live-verified returning 200 with no auth on the LAN — the clearest proof of the trusted-clients posture.
http_endpoints.name: List Files

http_endpoints.description: Moonraker-registered webcams. IMPORTANT: on stock U1 firmware the built-in camera is NOT a registered webcam — this list is empty (live-verified empty on a unit that HAS a working camera). The stock camera is served through the Snapmaker daemon path in the `camera` block below, not here. On third-party extended firmware this list populates with real webrtc/mjpeg entries.
http_endpoints.name: List Webcams

http_endpoints.description: Single JPEG frame from the built-in camera. Only refreshes while a monitor session is held open via the WebSocket camera.start_monitor call (see the `camera` block). Live-verified: after start_monitor, polling this returns ~93 KB image/jpeg frames that change frame to frame. Unauthenticated on the LAN.
http_endpoints.name: Camera Frame (stock)

http_endpoints.description: Past jobs, newest first (params: limit, start, order). Each job carries filename, status (completed/cancelled/...), start/end time, and metadata.thumbnails[] (fetch a thumbnail at /server/files/gcodes/<relative_path>). Live-verified (3 completed jobs with 3 thumbnails each). Pair with print/start to reprint without re-uploading.
http_endpoints.name: Print History

http_endpoints.description: Stop the current print. No body/params; returns {\"result\":\"ok\"}. HTTP-allowed and unauthenticated on the LAN. Siblings /printer/print/pause and /printer/print/resume behave the same. This is the correct 'stop' button — NOT emergency_stop (which on the U1 is WebSocket-only, JSON-RPC printer.emergency_stop, and needs a firmware_restart to recover). Advanced (halts a running print) but documented from the Snapmaker fork + upstream; not exercised here (no active print to cancel)."
http_endpoints.name: Cancel Print

http_endpoints.description: Start printing a file already on the printer: query param filename=<path relative to the gcodes root, from /server/files/list or history>. This is the reprint path — no re-upload. Requires the printer to be READY (not printing/paused). JSON-RPC printer.print.start {filename}. This is exactly the call Snapmaker's own Orca sends. Live-verified read side (the 7 gcode filenames it accepts were listed); the start itself was not triggered (someone else's printer). Advanced.
http_endpoints.name: Start / Reprint

http_endpoints.description: Multipart upload (file, path, print=true|false) to submit a NEW sliced job; start-after-upload when print=true. Orca retries on port 8080. Advanced: out of scope for the phone app (reprint from history is the intended flow); leads to printing.
http_endpoints.name: Upload File
